subtopic_detail: Endometrial cancer suspicion in postmenopausal bleeding with atrophic ultrasound
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 63 year old woman who reports a single episode of light postmenopausal per vaginum bleeding 3 days ago on a background of 12 years of amenorrhoea. She has hypertension controlled on perindopril and takes oral tamoxifen 20 mg daily for the last 18 months following breast cancer surgery. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin.

On examination the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Speculum shows an atrophic-appearing cervix with no visible cause for the bleed. Bimanual examination reveals a small anteverted mobile uterus and no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a homogenous endometrial thickness of 3 mm with no cystic changes and no adnexal abnormality. Cervical screening is up to date and normal.

data_table.Presenting complaint: Single episode of light PMB 3 days ago; 12 years amenorrhoea
data_table.Risk factors: BMI 32; T2DM on metformin; tamoxifen 20 mg for 18 months
data_table.Examination: Atrophic cervix; small mobile uterus; no adnexal mass
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Endometrium 3 mm homogenous; no cystic change; no adnexal abnormality
data_table.Screening: Cervical screening up to date and normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream for 6 weeks and review if bleeding recurs
options.rationale: Empirical topical oestrogen without excluding malignancy delays diagnosis; RANZCOG requires tissue sampling first regardless of the presumptive diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Reassure the patient and arrange follow-up if there is any further vaginal bleeding
options.rationale: Reassurance without tissue diagnosis is inadequate for postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen because the 3 mm threshold does not apply; a single episode still mandates further investigation (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to look for interval endometrial thickening
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound is not appropriate for postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen; the risk of missing endometrial carcinoma or hyperplasia is too high to defer tissue sampling (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Order a serum CA-125 and defer further investigation until the result is available
options.rationale: CA-125 is neither sensitive nor specific for endometrial cancer and does not substitute for histology; RANZCOG does not include CA-125 in the PMB pathway (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy despite an endometrial thickness of 3 mm
options.rationale: In women on tamoxifen the endometrial ultrasound thickness threshold is unreliable because tamoxifen produces subendothelial cystic changes that mimic thin atrophic endometrium; RANZCOG mandates hysteroscopy and biopsy for postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen regardless of ultrasound thickness (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. In women not on tamoxifen an endometrial thickness under 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound has a negative predictive value of about 99 percent, so pipelle biopsy is deferred if bleeding does not recur. Tamoxifen changes this rule: subendothelial cystic changes make ultrasound thickness unreliable, so tissue diagnosis by hysteroscopy and biopsy is required regardless of the ultrasound. Obesity and diabetes add background endometrial cancer risk. Deferring investigation for oestrogen cream, serial imaging, or serum markers misses malignancy.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen requires hysteroscopy and biopsy regardless of endometrial thickness
The 4 mm ultrasound threshold is only valid for women not on tamoxifen
Serum CA-125 and topical oestrogen do not substitute for tissue diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Tamoxifen produces subendothelial cysts that read as artefactually thin or thick endometrium; the ultrasound cannot rule out cancer, only histology can.

sources.label: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

subtopic_detail: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy choice with hepatic impairment
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar seeing a 54 year old man 10 days after completing a medically supervised inpatient alcohol withdrawal. His usual pattern before admission was 15 standard drinks daily for over a decade. He is highly motivated to stay abstinent and lives with his supportive wife. He is not on opioid pain relief and has no personal or family history of seizures.

Investigations from admission show ALT 96 U/L (under 40), AST 128 U/L (under 40), gamma-GT 320 U/L (under 60), bilirubin 26 micromol/L (under 20), albumin 34 g/L (33 to 47), INR 1.1, platelets 132 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), and a FibroScan reports significant liver fibrosis without established cirrhosis. eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m2. His BMI is 26 kg/m2 and there is no ascites or peripheral oedema. He has not previously tried any relapse prevention medication.

data_table.Alcohol history: 15 standard drinks daily for over a decade; 10 days abstinent post-withdrawal
data_table.LFTs: ALT 96; AST 128; gamma-GT 320; bilirubin 26; albumin 34; INR 1.1; platelets 132
data_table.Support: Living with supportive wife; not on opioids; no seizure history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate relapse prevention pharmacotherapy to commence?

options.text: Oral acamprosate 666 mg three times daily as first-line maintenance in significant liver fibrosis
options.rationale: Acamprosate is renally excreted and preferred over naltrexone when there is significant hepatic impairment; it is safe in liver disease as long as renal function is adequate and reduces relapse to heavy drinking (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oral disulfiram 200 mg daily under supervised administration by his wife
options.rationale: Disulfiram is contraindicated in significant liver disease because of the risk of severe hepatotoxicity and requires strict abstinence; it is not first-line and is unsafe with these LFTs (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oral gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrated to 600 mg three times daily as sole therapy
options.rationale: Gabapentin has limited evidence for alcohol use disorder relapse prevention and is not a first-line agent in AU practice; acamprosate or naltrexone are the recommended options (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oral naltrexone 50 mg daily starting today with LFT monitoring at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and carries a black box warning of hepatotoxicity in advanced liver disease; with AST double the upper reference range and significant fibrosis, acamprosate is safer (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Continued oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily as chronic maintenance to prevent relapse
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have no role in relapse prevention beyond the acute withdrawal window and expose him to cross-dependence and withdrawal reinstatement risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder in AU practice centres on acamprosate and naltrexone with disulfiram as an adjunct in highly selected patients. Acamprosate is renally cleared and is preferred when there is significant liver disease; naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and contraindicated in acute hepatitis or advanced liver failure. Disulfiram is contraindicated in significant liver disease. Benzodiazepines have no role beyond acute withdrawal. Gabapentin has limited evidence and is not first-line.
key_points: Acamprosate preferred when significant hepatic impairment coexists with alcohol use disorder
Naltrexone contraindicated in acute hepatitis or advanced liver failure
Disulfiram is not first-line and requires excellent adherence and no hepatic risk
explanation.pearls: The renal versus hepatic clearance profile of acamprosate versus naltrexone decides the choice more often than efficacy; check eGFR and LFTs before either prescription.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners AOD Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression pharmacotherapy in a breastfeeding woman
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman at her 8 week postnatal check. She reports 6 weeks of persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and thoughts that her baby would be better off without her. She denies any active plans to harm herself or the baby. Her EPDS score is 21 and she is exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term infant. She had a similar depressive episode after her first child that responded to sertraline.

She has no other medical history and is on no regular medications. She is engaged with the maternal and child health nurse and her partner is supportive and home each evening. She would like to continue breastfeeding and asks whether medication is compatible.

data_table.Presentation: 6 weeks persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep independent of baby
data_table.Passive suicidality: Thoughts baby would be better off without her; no active plan or intent
data_table.EPDS score: 21 with item 10 marked as denying active plans
data_table.Feeding: Exclusive breastfeeding of healthy term infant
data_table.History: Previous PND responded well to sertraline
data_table.Supports: Engaged with MCH nurse; supportive partner

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding and commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily as the primary antidepressant
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a longer half-life and higher relative infant dose than sertraline and is not first-line in breastfeeding; stopping breastfeeding is not needed when a compatible SSRI exists (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange inpatient mother-baby unit admission today for severe postnatal depression
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for women with active suicidal or infanticidal intent, psychosis, or inability to care for the infant; this woman has passive ideation only and strong community supports and can be managed in the community with escalation criteria (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily uptitrated to 50 to 100 mg daily and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding women because of the lowest relative infant dose and best safety data, and her prior treatment response makes it the appropriate agent; breastfeeding does not need to be interrupted (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone without pharmacotherapy for the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Moderate to severe postnatal depression (EPDS 21 with passive suicidal ideation) warrants pharmacotherapy with psychological therapy in parallel; therapy alone is inadequate at this severity (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night to address the sleep disturbance and review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line for postnatal depression, sedate infants through breastmilk, and do not treat the underlying mood disorder (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Moderate to severe postnatal depression requires combined pharmacotherapy and psychological treatment. Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding because its relative infant dose is under 2 percent and the safety data is the largest of the class. A prior therapeutic response is a strong indication to use the same drug. Fluoxetine is second-line because of a longer half-life and higher relative infant dose. Inpatient mother-baby unit admission is reserved for active suicidality, infanticidal intent, psychosis, or inability to care for the infant; passive ideation with strong supports is managed in the community with a clear escalation plan.
key_points: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding; do not interrupt breastfeeding
Combined SSRI plus psychological therapy for moderate to severe postnatal depression
Inpatient care reserved for active suicidality, infanticidal intent, or psychosis
explanation.pearls: EPDS item 10 (self-harm thoughts) is the trigger for direct safety enquiry; any positive answer needs a clear plan even when the total score is not extreme.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team commencing clozapine on a 32 year old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine. He is registered with a clozapine monitoring program. He lives independently with his mother and has weekly community mental health contact. He has no medical comorbidities and no family history of blood dyscrasias.

Baseline investigations before starting: white cell count 6.4 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), absolute neutrophil count 3.8 x 10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), haemoglobin 148 g/L (135 to 175), platelets 260 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L, ECG showing sinus rhythm with QTc 420 ms. He is not febrile and there are no signs of infection.

data_table.Diagnosis: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failed risperidone and olanzapine
data_table.Baseline FBC: WCC 6.4; ANC 3.8; Hb 148; platelets 260 (all within reference)
data_table.Metabolic and cardiac: Fasting glucose 4.6; ECG sinus with QTc 420 ms
data_table.Support and monitoring: Community mental health weekly; registered clozapine monitoring program

lead_in: What is the most appropriate schedule for full blood count monitoring in the first year of clozapine therapy?

options.text: Daily neutrophil count for the first 2 weeks then weekly for the remainder of the first year
options.rationale: Daily monitoring is disproportionate to the risk profile and imposes an impractical burden without changing detection of the true onset window of neutropenia which is weeks 6 to 18 (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Full blood count only when clinical symptoms of infection develop during therapy
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered monitoring alone misses asymptomatic neutropenia and does not meet program requirements; clozapine dispensing requires the FBC to be checked on schedule (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Weekly full blood count for 4 weeks then monthly thereafter for the duration of treatment
options.rationale: This underscreens for clozapine-induced neutropenia, which peaks in the 6 to 18 week window; the AU program requires weekly to 18 weeks (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Weekly full blood count for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly ongoing
options.rationale: The Australian clozapine monitoring program requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly indefinitely; this reflects the temporal risk of clozapine-induced neutropenia (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Fortnightly full blood count from the outset then monthly after 12 months of treatment
options.rationale: Fortnightly from the outset misses the highest risk window; weekly for 18 weeks is mandated at the start of therapy (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a small but persistent risk of neutropenia and agranulocytosis, peaking in the 6 to 18 week window. The Australian clozapine monitoring program requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 52 weeks, and monthly indefinitely; dispensing is contingent on the FBC. Fever should also trigger an FBC regardless of schedule. Baseline metabolic and cardiac assessment is done before commencement and repeated at 3 to 6 months. The other main monitoring risks are cardiac (myocarditis in the first 3 months) and constipation-related ileus.
key_points: Clozapine monitoring: weekly FBC for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly
Fever mandates an unscheduled FBC regardless of last check
Baseline and follow-up ECG, troponin, and metabolic parameters at 3 to 6 months
explanation.pearls: Clozapine dispensing in Australia is program-linked; the pharmacy cannot dispense unless the FBC has been submitted and cleared in the last week.

sources.label: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Generalised anxiety disorder first-line pharmacotherapy in an older adult
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 74 year old woman with 6 months of persistent worry about her adult children, restlessness, muscle tension, difficulty falling asleep, and irritability that has curtailed her activities. She lives alone and has hypertension well controlled on perindopril. She has osteopenia but no other medical comorbidities. Her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min and her sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145). She is not on any regular psychotropic medication.

Her GAD-7 score is 15 and PHQ-9 is 6. She has never had suicidal thoughts. She is otherwise engaged, cognitively intact on brief bedside testing, and reports no falls in the last year. She has read patient information on cognitive behavioural therapy and is willing to try either medication or therapy, and can access both.

data_table.Presentation: 6 months of worry, restlessness, muscle tension, insomnia, irritability
data_table.Comorbidities: Hypertension on perindopril; osteopenia; no falls in past year
data_table.Function: Cognitively intact; lives alone; activities curtailed by worry

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medication to consider?

options.text: Oral escitalopram 5 mg daily uptitrated to 10 mg with 2 week review and sodium check at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Escitalopram is first-line for generalised anxiety disorder in Australia with strong efficacy data; in older adults the starting dose is halved to 5 mg with a cap of 10 mg (QT and hyponatraemia risk), and sodium is checked at 4 weeks because SSRI hyponatraemia risk rises with age (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral amitriptyline 25 mg at night uptitrated as needed for anxiety and sleep
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are anticholinergic and pro-arrhythmic and are on the Beers list to avoid in older adults; they are not first-line for GAD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral pregabalin 75 mg twice daily titrated to 150 mg twice daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Pregabalin is second-line for GAD in AU practice with dose adjustment needed in reduced eGFR and a growing recognition of dependence; SSRI is tried first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral diazepam 5 mg twice daily as ongoing maintenance therapy for the anxiety symptoms
options.rationale: Chronic benzodiazepines in older adults are avoided per the Beers criteria because of falls, cognitive impairment, and dependence; short courses only during SSRI initiation are acceptable but not as maintenance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral quetiapine 25 mg at night titrated to 100 mg for anxiolysis and sleep
options.rationale: Quetiapine is not first-line for GAD, carries metabolic and QT risks, and is associated with excess mortality in older adults when used for behavioural symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder in an older adult should be treated with combined SSRI and cognitive behavioural therapy when both are accessible. Escitalopram is first-line with the starting dose halved (5 mg) and a cap of 10 mg in over-65s because of QT prolongation and hyponatraemia risk; sodium is checked at 4 weeks and any symptom of hyponatraemia (headache, confusion, seizure) prompts immediate assessment. Chronic benzodiazepines and tricyclics are on the Beers list. Quetiapine has metabolic and mortality signals in older adults. Pregabalin is second-line.
key_points: SSRI (escitalopram) first-line for GAD across age groups
Older adult escitalopram cap 10 mg per PBS/TGA to reduce QT prolongation
Check sodium at 4 weeks after SSRI initiation in older adults
explanation.pearls: SSRI-induced hyponatraemia typically appears within the first month; older women with low body weight are the highest-risk group and warrant a scheduled sodium recheck.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine Position Statement on Prescribing
